concerns: Assay sensitivity and false negatives: low-biomass nasal lavage/CSF matrices frequently yield poor recovery; without validated spike-in recovery in those exact matrices, a negative orthogonal detection result could reflect assay failure rather than absence of intact EV exposure (ev-misev2023-quality-framework; ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution).

Co-recovery of soluble factors: particle-enriched fractions can retain or co-isolate soluble secretome components that mediate bioactivity; detergent/protease pre-treatment and capture-depletion are essential but must be shown not to introduce assay artifacts (ev-misev2023-quality-framework; ev-hermann-2023-neonatal-hi).

Species and delivery limitations: positive rodent intranasal efficacy reports (ev-kodali-2017-status-epilepticus; ev-hermann-2023-neonatal-hi; ev-zhuang-2011-intranasal-exosome) do not guarantee similar intact-EV exposure in larger species; macaque data report negligible brain uptake and strong nasal retention after intranasal EV dosing, raising concern that delivery/formulation or species clearance may limit generalizability (ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution).

Detergent/protease controls interpretation: membrane-disruption may alter presentation of non-EV cargo (e.g., protein aggregates, lipoproteins) or change matrix interactions; appropriate buffer and reagent controls are necessary to avoid misattributing loss-of-function to EV-specificity (ev-misev2023-quality-framework).

Ex vivo assay specificity and sensitivity: the microglia LPS-cytokine readout must be validated to respond selectively to EV-associated cargo at expected concentrations and to be robust to potential carryover of capture reagents or detergents; otherwise, positive or negative functional readouts may be confounded (ev-misev2023-quality-framework).

Capture-depletion feasibility: practical removal of capture-positive particles from a particle-count–matched preparation may be challenging; inability to achieve true capture-negative but particle-matched arms would weaken discrimination between intact-EV and particle-count/secretome explanations (ev-misev2023-quality-framework).
conclusion: The proposed in vivo→ex vivo bridging experiment is conceptually sound and addresses a key translational gap: whether an orthogonally verified, membrane-protected EV fraction is necessary for short-interval CNS pharmacodynamic modulation after intranasal dosing. It aligns with MISEV2023 recommendations for orthogonal characterization and controls and leverages prior rodent intranasal efficacy reports as motivating precedent. The design includes important falsification controls (detergent/protease, capture-depletion, spike-in tracer) and a direct functional readout that can discriminate intact-EV dependence from secretome-driven effects. However, causal linkage is still high-risk: assay sensitivity, capture-reagent performance in low-biomass matrices, co-recovery of soluble factors, and species- or formulation-dependent delivery limit confidence in translation. If implemented with rigorous spike-in validation, orthogonal readouts, and sufficient biological replication, the experiment should discriminate the competing explanations enumerated in the proposal; negative outcomes will be interpretable only if spike-in and recovery controls perform reliably.
evidence_gap: Critical experimental-validation gaps remain: (1) demonstration that the chosen spike-in tracer and immuno-capture reagents reliably recover and distinguish membrane-protected EVs from soluble secretome in the same low-biomass matrices expected post-dosing (nasal lavage/CSF/olfactory mucosa); (2) feasibility data showing capture-depletion can remove capture-positive material without altering other matrix components; (3) dose/formulation/device parameters that achieve detectable orthogonal EV signal in vivo in rodents and predictably scale toward larger species; (4) evidence that the short-interval ex vivo microglia assay is sensitive and specific to EV-associated cargo versus co-recovered soluble factors.
